assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices made a clean, tunable many-body quantum system: the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, single-site-resolved microscopy and quantum gas microscopes, and engineered Hubbard models. It opened a regime in which strongly correlated quantum matter can be built and observed in detail, and it is a platform that has been reproduced and extended in many laboratories.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and colleagues) supplied the theoretical proposal for Hubbard physics with cold atoms; Greiner (Mott transition, with Hansch and Bloch) and Bloch (lattice experiments and quantum gas microscopy) carried the decisive experiments. Esslinger (fermionic Hubbard, Fermi gases in lattices) is also strong, so the three-name limit forces a difficult choice; Greiner's early contribution is the sharpest, with the theory-experiment pairing fitting a fair configuration.
assessment.maturity: Mature, robustly confirmed by many independent groups over more than twenty years, and the interpretation is stable. Recognition is fully timely. Partially adjacent to the 2001 BEC prize, but the discovery here is distinct.
uncertainties: Whether Esslinger or Jaksch deserves a seat over a listed name; the three-person cap makes the allocation contestable.
I rely on recollection for the exact credit split between the original theory proposal and the first experiments and have not verified it independently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock combines the magic-wavelength idea with many atoms to reach fractional uncertainty around 1e-18, which beats the microwave definition of the second by orders of magnitude. It is a decisive demonstration of precision quantum measurement, enabling tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a path to redefining the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated early realizations; Ye's group pushed the stability and accuracy to record levels and added many-body control. Both are widely seen as the decisive contributors, and a two-person prize is clean. Hall and Hansch were already recognized in 2005 for the frequency comb, which is a different invention.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many labs with independent clocks and comparisons. The redefinition of the second is still pending, but the underlying invention and its performance are firmly established and recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer to wait for the SI second redefinition as a marker of impact.
Whether additional contributors (for example Ludlow, Hinkley, Ye-group collaborators, or Takamoto) merit mention is not resolvable from the supplied credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made the strong coupling of microwave photons to superconducting artificial atoms routine and controlled, and it is the basis for dispersive readout, quantum-limited amplification context, and multi-qubit processors. As a theorist embedded in this field I judge it very important, but my judgement here is shaped by closeness to the subject and I flag possible conflict-of-interest.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and collaborators (Huang, Majer, Wallraff-style experiments) proposed the architecture; Schoelkopf's group and the Wallraff group demonstrated strong coupling. Wallraff, an experimental pioneer, is not in the credited names, which leaves a real allocation problem within this candidate. The list gives theory-heavy credit with Schoelkopf as the experimental anchor.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and independently confirmed in many laboratories. However, the 2025 prize recognized macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, so recognition of a closely related area immediately after it may be seen as premature or redundant by colleagues.
uncertainties: Timing relative to the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits.
Wallraff's omission from the credited names weakens the fairness of the configuration.
Possible conflict of interest through my work in the field and my WACQT role.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84 and related protocols founded quantum cryptography, turning the no-cloning and measurement-disturbance properties of quantum mechanics into a security principle, and launched practical quantum key distribution. The conceptual originality is high and it links to the foundational quantum information work already honoured in 2022.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard are the originators of BB84; Ekert's 1991 entanglement-based protocol is an independent and important contribution, so the credit is delicate, and I prefer the cleaner two-person configuration. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea, which is not in the list, complicates the narrative.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally mature, with satellite and fiber demonstrations and commercial systems, but practical security against device imperfections remains an active research issue. Fundamental impact is long established.
uncertainties: Ekert's role versus Bennett-Brassard and the omitted Wiesner priority.
Whether the discovery is physics enough for a physics prize versus computer science and cryptography.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light underpins quantum-enhanced interferometry: Caves provided the theoretical case for squeezed vacuum injection, Kimble's group made the first observations of squeezing in the laboratory, and Schnabel's group developed squeezed light for gravitational-wave detectors. It is a clear case where a quantum resource improves a real instrument, notably in LIGO and Virgo.
assessment.attribution: The attribution is plausible but the experimental history is shared: Slusher et al. and Wu, Kimble and colleagues first observed squeezing, and the engineering for gravitational-wave detectors involved large collaborations including the GEO600 and LIGO teams. A fair three-person configuration exists but is not unique.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed in operating gravitational-wave detectors, and mature. Recognition would be timely as a quantum-optics prize that links to the 2017 gravitational-wave prize.
uncertainties: The discovery-versus-engineering boundary and the precise first-observation credit.
Whether Slusher or other early experimentalists should replace a listed name; this is outside the supplied exact names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene revealed flat bands with correlated insulating states and unconventional superconductivity, and it created moire quantum matter as a whole new tunable materials platform. The prediction was theoretical and the experimental confirmation striking and clean, which is the kind of discovery that opens a regime of physics.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the magic angle and flat bands; Jarillo-Herrero's group demonstrated the correlated and superconducting phases. The omitted experimental collaborators (the first-author student group, and Dean and others working on moire platforms) and the shared theory credit leave open allocation questions, though the theory-experiment pairing is natural.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups with an active field of follow-ups, but the nature of the superconducting pairing and the role of sample-dependent disorder are still under debate, so the interpretation is not fully stable. Timing is reasonable but a little early.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of the superconductivity remains unresolved.
Whether Bistritzer or an omitted experimentalist is the better third seat; I defer to colleagues in materials physics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators established a new class of band structure with protected edge states, and it was confirmed by transport in HgTe quantum wells. The idea is conceptually original and has strongly influenced the search for topological quantum matter, though it follows the 2016 Nobel Prize on topological phases.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele proposed the quantum spin Hall effect in graphene; Molenkamp's group made the decisive HgTe experiments following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction. The omitted BHZ theorists and the Moore-Balents and Fu-Kane work on three-dimensional topological insulators make the credit inherently contested.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed independently, mature and very widely applied. The earlier 2016 prize on topological phase transitions could reduce the urgency.
uncertainties: Allocation among Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, and the 3D topological-insulator discoverers.
Outside my core expertise, so I defer to colleagues in condensed matter.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics brought mechanical motion into the quantum regime through radiation-pressure coupling, sideband cooling to the ground state, and optomechanical entanglement and squeezing, and it connects naturally to my interest in phonons and artificial atoms. It is a general platform with applications in sensing and transduction.
assessment.attribution: Kippenberg and Vahala demonstrated the early radiation-pressure effects in microresonators; Aspelmeyer's group pushed to quantum control and the macroscopic quantum regime. Many other groups (for example Harris, Painter, Lehnert, Schwab) made decisive ground-state and microwave-regime contributions, so the three listed names are not obviously the decisive set.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in multiple platforms, but its major impact is more as a technique and platform than a single discovery, and quantum applications are still developing, so recognition may be a little premature.
uncertainties: Whether the decisive contributions are shared with many other groups beyond the three credited names.
Whether it is a single discovery or a field of techniques.
